title: Flagpole Sitting: A Real Fad
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history of flagpole sitting as a 1920s fad, starting with Alvin "Shipwreck" Kelly's 13-hour sit and his later record sits. They connect it to the dance marathon craze (Alma Cummings), the Depression-era endurance contests, and later flagpole sitters including Dixie Blandy, Kenneth Gidge, and David Werder. The episode opens with book pre-order promotion and banter, includes ad breaks, and closes with listener mail about doctor names.

segments.title: Book pre-order promo and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh promotes the upcoming Stuff You Should Know book and pre-order gift, then the hosts chat about a former show's theme song, Josh's lawnmower, and the band Harvey Danger.

segments.title: Introduction to flagpole sitting
segments.summary: The hosts introduce flagpole sitting as a bizarre 1920s fad, describing the modified flagpole with a bar-stool-like seat and noting that sitting on top of a pole for as long as possible defines it.

segments.title: Shipwreck Kelly's early life and nickname
segments.summary: Alvin Kelly's biography is covered: born in Hell's Kitchen, orphaned early, a steeplejack and sailor, World War One naval service, and the origin of the nickname shipwreck, which is disputed and possibly embellished.
topics: World War One Naval Auxiliary Reserve

segments.title: Kelly's first sit and the flagpole craze
segments.summary: Kelly's first major sit of thirteen hours and thirteen minutes is described, with disputed locations (Hollywood or a Philadelphia department store). The record-breaking spread of the fad and the 1920s appetite for fads are discussed.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: A sponsor break separates the flagpole segment from the dance marathon discussion.

segments.title: Dance marathons and Alma Cummings
segments.summary: Dance marathons are introduced as a parallel 1920s endurance fad, starting with Alma Cummings' 27-hour dance in 1923 and the wider craze for endurance challenges. The hosts note the hunger for fame behind them.

segments.title: Depression-era dance marathons and their cruelty
segments.summary: Dance marathons during the Depression are described: contestants competed for food, shelter, and prize money, and rules tightened over time so rest was cut to minutes per hour. The hosts criticize the promoters and the crowds.

segments.title: Shipwreck Kelly's record sits and money-making
segments.summary: Kelly's longer sits are listed, including 146 hours in Kansas City, 312 hours in Newark, and a 22-day sit tied to a Madison Square Garden dance marathon. Methods of sleeping, toilet arrangements, and his earnings are covered. The Depression and public backlash are covered, including an arrest in the Bronx.

segments.title: Kelly's decline and later life
segments.summary: Kelly's fall from fame, his final sit in Orange, Texas in 1952, two heart attacks, and his death on a New York sidewalk are described. His later work as a dancer at the Roseland Ballroom is mentioned.

segments.title: Later flagpole sitters and records
segments.summary: Dixie Blandy's career and fatal fall in 1974 in Pennsylvania are covered, along with other stunts: Santa-costumed Christmas sitter, Peggy Townsend, Kenneth Gidge's 248-day sit, and David Werder's 439-day protest sit, plus David Blaine's 35-hour standing stunt.
